title: US Tech Companies Just Cut 38,000 Jobs in a Single Month. Indian Workers Are in the Crossfire.
excerpt: May's tech layoffs were the highest in nearly two years, driven by AI investment and efficiency pushes. With 123,000 cuts so far in 2026, H-1B holders and Indian IT workers face a tightening market on both sides of the Pacific.
body:
American technology companies announced 38,242 job cuts in May — the highest monthly total since August 2024 — as the industry's spending on artificial intelligence accelerates a structural reshaping of its workforce. The data, published by outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas, shows that the tech sector has announced 123,653 cuts in the first five months of 2026, a staggering 65 percent increase over the same period last year.

The numbers land at a moment when Indian tech workers, both in the United States and in India, are caught in a tightening vice. On one side, American companies are shedding roles that AI tools can increasingly perform. On the other, Indian IT giants that have historically absorbed displaced talent are themselves contracting.

## The AI Restructuring

The layoffs are not a cyclical downturn. They are a structural reset driven by the rapid integration of AI into software development, customer service, data analysis, and back-office operations. Companies are investing billions in AI infrastructure while simultaneously reducing the human workforce those investments are designed to replace.

"This is less a temporary downturn and more a structural reset," one technology executive noted on LinkedIn. "The headlines may become less dramatic, but the pressure on tech employment probably isn't going away anytime soon."

The pattern is visible across the industry. T-Mobile, which has been steadily laying off American workers through 2025 and 2026, recently opened a new office in Hyderabad through its affiliate TMUS Global Solutions. While T-Mobile clarified that the Hyderabad expansion involved converting existing contractors to employees — not shifting US roles offshore — the optics of simultaneous US layoffs and Indian hiring have drawn scrutiny.

T-Mobile said its "technology and IT work remains centered in the US" and that TMUS Global Solutions "supports internal technology and engineering functions and does not provide customer-facing services." But the broader trend it represents — American companies reducing domestic headcount while maintaining or expanding operations in lower-cost markets — is unmistakable.

## The Indian IT Squeeze

The pain extends to India's homegrown IT sector. Reliance Industries, the country's largest private employer with over 419,000 staff, saw headcount growth slow to 4 percent year-on-year as of March 2026 — one quarter of its expansion rate the previous year. The company's annual report has turned hazier on workforce breakdowns, discontinuing a detailed table of employees across business divisions.

At Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys, employee counts are now up to 5 percent below their respective March 2023 peaks. Revenue growth has slowed, and AI-powered coding tools are reducing the need for the large teams that once defined Indian IT outsourcing.

India's Chief Economic Advisor V. Anantha Nageswaran warned in February that future job growth, not headline layoffs, is the bigger concern. His call for the private sector to hire more and balance capital-intensive growth with labour-intensive growth has gone unanswered. Urban youth unemployment stands at 13.6 percent, and it is now common for college graduates to queue up for janitorial roles in the public sector.

## What H-1B Holders Face

For the estimated 600,000 Indian nationals on H-1B visas in the United States, the layoff surge creates an acute vulnerability. H-1B holders who lose their jobs have a 60-day grace period to find new employment or leave the country. In a market where 38,000 tech roles disappeared in a single month, that window is increasingly difficult to use.

The immigration dimension compounds the problem. The Trump administration's heightened scrutiny of visa programmes, combined with the ICE investigation into 10,000 cases of OPT fraud announced this week, has created an atmosphere of uncertainty around every work-authorisation category that Indian professionals rely on.

Fresh graduates are equally exposed. Campus hiring by major IT companies has been frozen or reduced, with joining dates delayed by six to ten months. Thousands of graduates from the 2023, 2024, and 2025 batches remain without placement — a bottleneck that is pushing families to reconsider the IT career path that lifted millions into the middle class over the past two decades.

## The Paradox of AI Spending

The layoffs exist alongside record investment. American technology companies are pouring tens of billions into data centres, AI chips, and large language model development. Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI training hardware, has seen its revenue surge. But the companies buying that hardware are simultaneously deciding they need fewer people to use it.

This creates a paradox for India. The country's AI talent pool is growing — IITs and private universities are expanding AI and machine learning programmes. But the jobs that AI creates tend to be fewer, more specialised, and higher-paying than the ones it eliminates. The broad-based employment that characterised the IT boom of the 2000s and 2010s is unlikely to return in the same form.

## What Comes Next

Total private-sector job cuts in the US are actually down 7 percent year-over-year, suggesting the broader economy is not in freefall. But the concentration of cuts in technology — the sector that employs the largest number of H-1B workers — means the impact on Indian professionals is disproportionate.

The question for the diaspora is not whether the AI transition will happen, but how quickly and how completely it will reshape the labour market that made the Indian-American professional class possible. The answer, based on the May data, is faster than most anticipated.
